title: Kriti Sanon approaches Delhi High Court seeking protection against AI-generated impersonation, unauthorised use of identity
raw_summary:
Bollywood actress Kriti Sanon has approached the Delhi High Court seeking protection of her personality and publicity rights against the alleged unauthorised use of her name, image, likeness and other aspects of her identity. Her plea also covers the alleged use of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content and digital impersonation.

The matter came up before a single-judge Bench of Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. During the hearing, the court asked Kriti's counsel to place on record relevant judgments, research papers and other material concerning the legal questions surrounding personality rights.

The High Court indicated that it would pass a comprehensive order after examining the judgments and research material submitted by the actress's legal team. The matter has now been listed for further hearing on October 29. Kriti Sanon seeks protection of her identity in the digital space Kriti's plea comes at a time when the unauthorised use of celebrities' identities through digital platforms has become an increasingly prominent legal issue. Apart from the unauthorised commercial use of names and images, courts are also dealing with cases involving AI-generated content, deepfakes, digital impersonation and fake endorsements.

Personality and publicity rights generally seek to protect aspects of an individual's identity from being commercially exploited or represented without authorisation. The growing use of generative AI has added another layer to these disputes, as digitally created images, videos and other content can closely imitate public figures.

The Delhi High Court has heard several cases in recent months involving celebrities and public figures seeking protection against such alleged misuse.

title: The best ending for Drishyam is NO Drishyam 4. Why Ajay Devgn and Abhishek Pathak are RIGHT to end the blockbuster franchise
raw_summary:
At a time when Bollywood is obsessed with franchises and cinematic universes, Drishyam: The Conclusion has proved that knowing when to end a successful story could be as important as knowing how to begin one.

The phenomenal success of Drishyam The Conclusion has once again demonstrated the extraordinary popularity of Ajay Devgn's Vijay Salgaonkar. Released on October 2, the suspense thriller has emerged as one of the biggest Bollywood successes of 2026, crossing the Rs. 500 crore mark at the worldwide box office. At a time when even star-studded entertainers are struggling to justify their budgets, Drishyam The Conclusion has proved that an engaging story, memorable characters and clever writing can still bring audiences to cinemas in huge numbers.

Going by conventional Bollywood logic, this should be the perfect opportunity to announce Drishyam 4. After all, why would any producer willingly discontinue a franchise capable of generating hundreds of crores?

Yet, director Abhishek Pathak has made it clear that the journey of Vijay Salgaonkar has reached its destination and that there are no plans for another instalment. It is a decision that deserves to be celebrated, not questioned. Because, sometimes, the smartest decision a filmmaker can make is to walk away from a goldmine. The Rs. 500 crore temptation

Let's face it. If Drishyam 4 were announced tomorrow, the trade would undoubtedly sit up and take notice. The combination of Ajay Devgn, Vijay Salgaonkar, October 2 and the promise of another mind-bending climax would be sufficient to generate enormous curiosity.

The producers already have something that filmmakers spend years trying to create: an established franchise with tremendous audience goodwill.

The first Drishyam (2015) gradually acquired a cult following, while Drishyam 2 (2022) emerged as a major theatrical success at a time when the Hindi film industry desperately needed reassurance that audiences were willing to return to cinemas. Drishyam The Conclusion has taken the franchise's commercial potential to an entirely different level.

Therefore, commercially speaking, making another instalment might appear to be a no-brainer.

But cinema cannot always be reduced to a balance sheet. There is a difference between a film making money because it has a compelling story and a film being made simply because there is money to be earned.

And that is precisely the trap which Drishyam must avoid.

The brilliance of Drishyam lies in its central premise. Vijay Salgaonkar is an ordinary family man blessed with extraordinary intelligence and an obsessive understanding of cinema. When his family faces an unimaginable crisis, he uses his knowledge, presence of mind and meticulous planning to protect his loved ones.

The character works because audiences identify with his circumstances, understand his desperation and are fascinated by his ability to remain several steps ahead of the investigating authorities.

But there is a limit to how many times the same formula can be repeated.

How many more investigations can Vijay outsmart? How many more officers can enter Goa determined to expose him? How many more times can audiences be asked to believe that the same family is caught in another elaborate cat-and-mouse game?

The first time, it was extraordinary. The second time, it was thrilling because the writers found an ingenious way to revisit the consequences of the original crime. The third film had the responsibility of bringing this remarkable journey to a satisfying conclusion.

A fourth instalment would face an even bigger challenge: justifying why a story that has already reached its conclusion needs to begin again.

There is also the danger of turning Vijay Salgaonkar into an almost superhuman figure. The character's greatest strength is that he is believable despite his extraordinary intelligence. If he continues to escape increasingly impossible circumstances, the franchise could eventually lose the very credibility that made it special.

Hindi cinema's growing dependence on established intellectual properties is understandable. Sequels offer brand recognition, relatively easier marketing and an audience already familiar with the characters.

But the success of a franchise should not automatically become a licence to extend it indefinitely.

Increasingly, Bollywood appears more interested in announcing the next instalment, spin-off or cinematic universe than allowing individual stories to breathe. Franchise-building is becoming an industrial strategy rather than a purely creative decision.

There is nothing inherently wrong with this approach. A well-written sequel can expand a fictional world and deliver an experience superior to its predecessor. However, the crucial question should always be whether the next film has a story worth telling.

Not whether the previous film collected Rs. 300 crores or Rs. 500 crores.

In that respect, the decision to conclude Drishyam is refreshing. It sends out a message that not every successful property needs to be exploited until audience enthusiasm disappears.

After all, the biggest threat to a beloved franchise is not necessarily a flop. Sometimes, it is one unnecessary sequel too many.

Sometimes, the best way to ensure that audiences remember a story forever is to resist the urge to keep telling it.

Drishyam has spent three films teaching us that Vijay Salgaonkar always knows how to stay one step ahead.

Perhaps the makers can take a lesson from their own protagonist and stay one step ahead of Bollywood's sequel obsession.

The audience may want Drishyam 4. The box office may justify Drishyam 4. But that doesn't mean Bollywood needs Drishyam 4.

title: Nitanshi Goel joins Korean skincare brand Mamonde as its first India brand ambassador
raw_summary:
Mamonde, the Korean skincare brand from the Amorepacific Group, has signed actor Nitanshi Goel as its first brand ambassador in India. The association marks an exciting next step for the brand, which launched exclusively on Nykaa in August 2026, as it brings its distinctive, flower-powered approach to skincare to a new generation of Indian beauty consumers.

Nitanshi captured the country’s attention with her breakout performance in Laapataa Ladies, winning hearts with her charm and natural screen presence. Now, she is stepping into the world of Korean beauty with Mamonde, a brand that pairs skincare science with the power of flowers. With young Indian consumers increasingly looking to K-beauty for innovative formulations and effective skincare, the partnership brings together a rising young star and a brand looking to make its mark in one of beauty’s most exciting categories.

“India’s beauty consumers are evolving quickly, and the relevance of Korean beauty among young people continues to grow. With Mamonde, we are bringing innovative, benefit-led skincare to India at accessible price points. Nitanshi’s youthful energy and relatability make her the ideal face to introduce Mamonde to the next generation of beauty consumers. This appointment reflects our long-term commitment to building Mamonde into a strong Korean skincare brand in India,” said Paul Lee, Managing Director & Country Head, Amorepacific India.

“Mamonde brings together Korean skincare expertise, targeted formulations and a fresh approach to everyday beauty. With Nitanshi on board, we have an opportunity to bring the brand closer to young consumers through campaigns and conversations that feel relevant to them. From discovering products for specific skin concerns to finding new favourites for their everyday routines, we want to make exploring Mamonde an exciting experience for India’s young beauty community,” added Mini Sood Banerjee, Deputy Director, Amorepacific India.

The partnership also brings Mamonde’s philosophy, ‘Let Your Skin Bloom’, to life. Rooted in the resilience and transformative power of flowers, the philosophy celebrates the idea that beauty is never one-size-fits-all. Just as every flower blooms differently, every individual has unique skin needs. Mamonde encourages consumers to embrace that individuality and discover skincare that works for them.

“I’m really excited to be joining Mamonde as its first brand ambassador in India. What drew me to the brand is how it combines Korean skincare innovation with a message that feels personal. ‘Let Your Skin Bloom’ is something I connect with because everyone’s skin is different, and skincare should be about discovering what makes you feel your best. I can’t wait to introduce more young people to Mamonde and be part of the brand’s journey in India,” said Nitanshi Goel.

Mamonde’s skincare range brings a targeted approach to everyday skin concerns. The Rose HA range, featuring a Serum and Sunscreen, focuses on hydration for a plump-looking, dewy complexion. The Peony BHA range, comprising a Serum and Sunscreen, addresses pore care and excess sebum management while providing UV protection. The range also features the Liquid Mask, a leave-on formula that combines gentle exfoliation with glow-enhancing benefits for an easy addition to everyday skincare routines.

With its first brand ambassador now on board, Mamonde is set to introduce more Indian consumers to its take on Korean skincare, with Nitanshi helping bring its ‘Let Your Skin Bloom’ philosophy to life.

title: Watch the drama, BUY the heroine's outfit! Microdramas cross 1 BILLION daily episode views as shopping enters the storyline
raw_summary:
India's microdrama revolution is entering an exciting new phase. After capturing audiences with bite-sized stories, dramatic twists and addictive cliffhangers, the rapidly growing entertainment format is now venturing into online shopping! ShareChat and Moj have introduced a new feature called 'Shop the Scene', which allows viewers to purchase products featured in their favourite microdramas while watching them.

The development comes at a time when microdramas are generating a staggering 1 billion episode views every day across the ShareChat network, according to figures shared by the company. The numbers underline the phenomenal popularity of vertical storytelling, which has emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of India's digital entertainment industry. However, the company-reported viewership figure has not been independently verified.

The most fascinating aspect of the new initiative is its potential to transform entertainment into a shopping experience. Imagine watching a romantic microdrama and instantly purchasing the outfit worn by the heroine. Or watching a family drama and ordering a product featured in a particular scene. With 'Shop the Scene', this concept is becoming a reality. The feature is currently being enabled through partnerships with two major e-commerce platforms, although their identities have not been revealed. But that's not all. ShareChat and Moj are also experimenting with advertisements featuring actors from the microdramas themselves. These advertisements are strategically placed between episodes, particularly at moments when a story reaches a dramatic cliffhanger. The idea is to make brand promotions feel like a natural extension of the entertainment rather than a conventional commercial break. According to ShareChat, such campaigns have recorded three times higher engagement and 1.5 times higher click-through rates, although the company has not disclosed the benchmarks against which these improvements were measured. Apart from 'Shop the Scene', the platforms have introduced other advertising innovations, including Regional AR Lens, Pincode Webcard and Superlikes, aimed at helping brands engage with audiences across different regions and markets.

The timing of these launches is significant. According to Kantar's State of Microdrama in India research, nearly 55% of surveyed microdrama viewers increase their consumption during the festive season. This presents an attractive opportunity for advertisers looking to reach consumers during India's biggest shopping period. For the entertainment industry, the implications could be substantial. Actors could find additional endorsement opportunities, production houses could explore branded storytelling, and microdrama creators could potentially generate revenue beyond advertising and subscriptions. However, the success of this model will ultimately depend on whether viewers actually purchase products while watching their favourite stories. For now, the initiative represents an interesting experiment in combining storytelling, advertising and e-commerce.

One thing is certain: India's microdrama business is no longer just about getting audiences hooked on the next episode. The next big cliffhanger could make viewers click not just 'Watch Next', but also 'Buy Now'!

Actor Imran Khan, an American citizen and Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, is set to challenge the Foreigners Regional Registration Office’s (FRRO) directive asking him to leave India by October 28, as per a report by NDTV. His lawyer, Zulfiqar Memon, will file a petition before the Bombay High Court contesting the order.

The actor came under scrutiny following his participation in a protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Mumbai. The demonstration called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Following the protest, BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party) leader Kirit Somaiya lodged a complaint with the police, alleging that Imran Khan’s participation in the demonstration violated the restrictions applicable to foreign citizens. The police subsequently forwarded the complaint to the FRRO, which issued a notice directing the actor to leave the country.

The FRRO’s position is that holding an OCI card does not permit a foreign national to participate in protests. The order has been issued under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. Section 7 of the legislation empowers the Central Government to issue orders and directions regulating, restricting or prohibiting the entry, departure, presence or movement of foreign nationals in India.

Meanwhile, veteran actor Raza Murad has slammed Khan, asserting that foreign nationals should not interfere in India’s domestic affairs. He also defended the authorities’ handling of the matter, pointing out that the actor has been given time to respond to the order and can seek judicial intervention if he believes the decision is unjust.

“Whether it is Imran Khan or anyone else, no foreign national has any business interfering in the internal affairs of our country. I have only just learned that Imran Khan has become a U.S. national; he was an actor here. As a U.S. national, he has no right to participate so actively in the country’s internal affairs or its politics. The Mumbai Police are acting strictly within the legal framework,” Murad told the news agency ANI.

He further noted that the actor has been given 15 days and can approach the court if he believes he is being treated unfairly or is being compelled to leave the country.

“He has been given a full 15 days. If he feels he is being treated unfairly or being forced to leave the country, he is welcome to approach the court, and whatever the court decides, we must all accept it. Let’s see how he reacts. He has two options: either leave the country by October 28, or if he does not wish to leave, or feels that he has been wronged or treated unjustly, he can take his grievance to the court,” Murad added.

Imran Khan’s proposed legal challenge will now bring the dispute before the Bombay High Court, where the validity of the FRRO’s order can be contested.

title: Kiss Ka Kissa: Vidhi Kasliwal announces romantic short film starring Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Josh
raw_summary:
In a city where couples can stay connected over their phones all day but struggle to find a few uninterrupted minutes together, even a simple kiss can turn into an adventure. Exploring this idea is Kiss Ka Kissa, an upcoming romantic Hindi short film starring real-life couple Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Joshi. Landmarc Entertainment, led by filmmaker-producer Vidhi Kasliwal, has announced that the film will be released on October 22, 2026.

Set in Mumbai, Kiss Ka Kissa explores the romantic dreams people carry from their younger days and the little moments that sometimes remain unfulfilled. Combining humour, affection and everyday situations, the film looks at modern relationships and the ways romance can be found in seemingly ordinary experiences.

The pairing of Priyanshu Painyuli and Vandana Joshi, who are also a couple in real life, brings an element of familiarity to the story. Rather than relying on grand romantic gestures, the film focuses on the emotions that emerge from everyday interactions. At its core, it celebrates spontaneity in love and the small moments that bring two people closer.

For Vidhi Kasliwal, the project continues her interest in stories centred on human emotions. Her filmmaking journey includes working with Rajshri Productions alongside Sooraj R. Barjatya before making her writing and directorial debut with Isi Life Mein.

"What drew me to Kiss Ka Kissa was its simplicity. We often associate romance with grand gestures, but sometimes the smallest moments carry the deepest emotions. There is something wonderfully relatable about two people trying to find a little space for themselves in a city that never slows down. At Landmarc, we have always believed that stories don't need to be larger than life to touch lives. They simply need to feel real," says Vidhi Kasliwal.

Written and directed by Ashish Sharma, Kiss Ka Kissa marks his fiction debut following more than a decade of work in advertising films, music videos and branded storytelling. The film is presented by Landmarc Entertainment and produced under its Landmarc Films banner. Vidhi Kasliwal has handled the production and creative direction, while Aarti Bagdi serves as the creative producer.

Speaking about the film, Ashish Sharma shares, "I wanted to make Kiss Ka Kissa for two reasons: the little romantic dreams we carry from our younger days, and the joy of telling a simple, feel-good story. A first kiss, a stolen moment, a romantic adventure—sometimes life moves on, leaving these little dreams unfinished. Set against the chaos of Mumbai, the film explores how even the simplest romantic gesture can become an adventure when privacy is a luxury. I wanted the humour to emerge naturally from everyday situations. At its heart, the film celebrates love, youthful innocence and life's delightful unpredictability. I hope it leaves audiences smiling and perhaps remembering a little unfinished romantic story of their own."

Over the past 15 years, Landmarc has developed a filmography that includes Sanngto Aika, Vazandar, Ringan, Gachchi, Redu, Pipsi, Nashibvaan and Medium Spicy. As the company transitions into Landmarc Entertainment, it is expanding its operations through three initial verticals: Landmarc Films, Landmarc Melodies and Landmarc Digital. The company aims to explore new storytelling formats and support new voices while continuing to focus on emotionally driven narratives.

The film's creative team includes Vidhi Kasliwal as producer and creative visionary, Ashish Sharma as director, Aarti Bagdi as creative producer, Vikrant Thakur as director of photography and Puloma Pal as editor. Sarthak Karkare has composed the music, written the lyrics and created the background score. Prince Kumar of Casting Cubicle is responsible for casting, while K. R. Mahadevan [Mohan] serves as executive producer.

With its title reflecting the story's central idea, Kiss Ka Kissa looks beyond the kiss itself to explore the circumstances surrounding it. Against the pace of Mumbai, the film highlights how finding time for romance can be challenging, and how a single moment can become meaningful when two people make the most of it.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Frontal nudity gets censor clearance! CBFC retains 2-second adult magazine shot in Doosra; Abhinay Deo calls it an “achievement”
raw_summary:
The trailer of Doosra, which was recently unveiled, has caught attention for its unusual storytelling. The film not only revisits Sourav Ganguly's iconic moment following India's historic victory over England in the 2002 NatWest Series final but also follows the parallel story of Tara (Plabita Borthakur), a young girl growing up in a deeply conservative household in Rajasthan. While films of this nature are usually expected to receive a 'U' or 'U/A' certificate, Doosra has been granted an 'A' certificate by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC). Interestingly, director Abhinay Deo willingly accepted the adult certification rather than agree to certain cuts. In an exclusive interview with Bollywood Hungama, the filmmaker revealed why he took this decision.

When asked about the certification Doosra received from the CBFC, Abhinay Deo said, "It’s an adult-rated movie due to a few scenes. I was there at the censor screening and they asked me, ‘What rating do you want?’. I suggested a U/A rating. They agreed but asked us to cut 3 scenes. I told them, ‘If we can get the film passed with an A-rating and without a cut, I won’t mind’. They said, ‘If you are okay with adult-rating, we won’t cut a single shot’. I agreed."

Abhinay Deo remarked, "It’s an achievement as nowadays, even films with ‘A’ have to go through cuts."

One of the scenes that contributed to the 'A' certification features Tara's father (Ankur Vikal) catching her with an adult magazine during her childhood. The sequence includes a clear, two-second shot of a nude photograph of a woman in the magazine. The CBFC has often been strict about the depiction of nudity on screen, with several films facing cuts over such content. However, in this case, the board allowed the shot to remain intact.

Abhinay Deo revealed, "Those 2-3 shots, which they wanted to cut, were integral to the film. One was the magazine shot. Then, we had a reference where we touched upon the Babri Masjid episode. They told me, ‘Thoda kam kar do, change kar do’. I confessed that I didn’t want to touch the film."

Was Abhinay Deo apprehensive about losing out on the under-18 audience because of the adult certification? He replied, "No, because this is not a film for teenagers to watch, though it is relevant to them."

Doosra is scheduled to release in cinemas on October 23.

The case relates to alleged obscene remarks made by Honey Singh during a concert in Delhi in January 2026. A video clip from the performance later circulated on social media and drew criticism from several users.

According to earlier reports, the remarks allegedly included an indecent reference to having sex in cars. Following the online backlash, a Mumbai resident approached the cyber police with a complaint, leading to the registration of a case.

Honey Singh subsequently issued a video apology, acknowledging that his choice of words had offended people. Explaining his intention behind the remarks, he said, "Seeing a larger number of Gen Z, I tried to convey a message in a language which they would prefer.
